concepts.title: Intelligence Quotient (IQ)
concepts.definition: A single numeric index of general mental ability that compares what a test-taker can do at present (mental age) with how long the person has actually lived (chronological age), scaled so that an age-typical performer lands at 100.
concepts.key_idea: Divide mental age by real age and multiply by 100; a result of 100 means performance typical of that age.
concepts.textbook_ref: lepy101.txt, Assessment of Intelligence (Stern's 1912 IQ concept, worked examples of 10-year-old children)
question_patterns: find the IQ of a child whose mental age and chronological age are given
a 10 year old shows a mental age of 12 - what is the child's intelligence quotient?
compute the IQ when MA equals 9 and CA equals 12
what does an IQ score of exactly 100 tell us about mental age relative to chronological age?
how is the intelligence quotient worked out from mental age and chronological age?
a 12-year-old obtains an IQ of 90 - determine the mental age this score implies

solution_steps.action: divide mental age by chronological age
solution_steps.explain: this ratio shows whether intellectual development runs ahead of or behind the age norm

solution_steps.action: multiply the ratio by 100
solution_steps.explain: the factor 100 keeps the quotient a whole-number style score instead of a decimal

worked_examples.q: A 10-year-old solves problems like a typical 12-year-old. Using mental age / real age * 100, what is the child's IQ?

concepts.title: IQ Classification Bands and Population Shares
concepts.definition: Because IQ scores pile up in the middle of a bell-shaped normal curve, psychologists label bands - average around 90-109, superior 120-130, borderline 70-79 - and can attach an approximate share of people to every band.
concepts.key_idea: Multiply the total population by a band's percentage share to estimate how many people fall in that IQ band.
concepts.textbook_ref: lepy101.txt, Table 1.1 classification of people on the basis of IQ (average 50.0, above 130 and below 70 about 2.2 each)
question_patterns: in a town of 20000 people how many are expected to lie in the average IQ band of 90 to 109?
what share of the population scores below IQ 70 on the normal curve of intelligence?
calculate the expected number of intellectually disabled persons in a district of 50000 using the IQ distribution
how many people out of one lakh would be expected to score above IQ 130?
state the IQ range labelled average and the percentage of people it covers
using the bell shaped spread of IQ scores, estimate the number of gifted children in a school population of 2500

solution_steps.action: multiply the population by the band percentage
solution_steps.explain: the share for each band, such as 50.0 for average or 2.2 for below 70, comes from the standard classification table

solution_steps.action: divide by 100 to convert percent into a head count
solution_steps.explain: a percentage must be scaled down to an actual number of people

worked_examples.q: An IQ score of 100 falls in which band: average, superior or borderline?

concepts.title: Intellectual Giftedness and Intellectual Disability
concepts.definition: The two tails of the IQ spread get special labels: beyond 130 sits giftedness, exceptional general ability shown across many areas, while below 70 the term intellectual disability applies only when sub-average functioning is joined by deficits in adaptive behaviour during the developmental years up to 18.
concepts.formula: iq_above_130 -> giftedness ; iq_below_70 plus adaptive_deficits within age_0_to_18 -> intellectual_disability
concepts.key_idea: A low score alone never settles disability - adaptive behaviour deficits before adulthood must accompany it; giftedness also differs from talent, which is narrow excellence in one field.
concepts.textbook_ref: lepy101.txt, Variations of Intelligence (AAMD three-feature definition, mild to profound levels, Terman's 1500-child study)
question_patterns: distinguish between intellectual giftedness and talent with one example of each
state the three defining features of intellectual disability in the AAMD formulation
why is an IQ below 70 by itself not enough to judge a child intellectually disabled?
list four characteristics commonly shown by gifted children in early childhood
name the four levels of intellectual disability together with their IQ ranges
what kind of educational programmes do gifted learners need beyond the regular classroom?

solution_steps.action: check both defining conditions for intellectual disability
solution_steps.explain: sub-average IQ must coexist with adaptive behaviour deficits observed during the developmental period between 0 and 18 years

solution_steps.action: contrast giftedness with talent
solution_steps.explain: giftedness is superior general ability across a wide variety of areas, whereas talent is remarkable ability confined to one specific field

worked_examples.q: Beyond which IQ score does giftedness begin?

concepts.title: Psychometric Theories and the Guilford Cell Count
concepts.definition: Structural theories treat intelligence as a set of measurable abilities: Spearman's general g-factor with specific s-factors derived through factor analysis, Thurstone's seven primary mental abilities, Jensen's Level I and Level II hierarchy, and Guilford's three-dimensional operations-contents-products model.
concepts.key_idea: Guilford crosses 6 operations with 5 contents and 6 products, so his structure-of-intellect model holds 180 ability cells.
concepts.textbook_ref: lepy101.txt, Theories of Intelligence (Spearman 1927, Thurstone seven primary abilities, Jensen Level I/II, Guilford 6x5x6 = 180 cells)
question_patterns: how many cells does the structure-of-intellect model contain when its three dimensions are multiplied?
explain Spearman's two-factor theory and the part played by factor analysis
list Thurstone's seven primary mental abilities with one phrase describing each
differentiate Level I associative learning from Level II cognitive competence in Jensen's hierarchical model
calculate the total number of categories in Guilford's model from its operations, contents and products dimensions
which statistical procedure did Spearman employ before proposing the g-factor?

solution_steps.action: multiply the number of operations by the number of contents
solution_steps.explain: each operation can combine with each content, so the pairs multiply

solution_steps.action: multiply that product by the number of product forms
solution_steps.explain: adding the third dimension of information products completes the classification cube

worked_examples.q: Guilford crosses 6 operations, 5 contents and 6 products. How many ability cells does his model hold?

concepts.title: Gardner's Theory of Multiple Intelligences
concepts.definition: Gardner replaces one general ability with eight relatively independent kinds - linguistic, logical-mathematical, spatial, musical, bodily-kinaesthetic, interpersonal, intrapersonal and naturalistic - so being strong in one tells you little about the rest.
concepts.formula: independent_intelligences = eight_types: linguistic, logical_mathematical, spatial, musical, bodily_kinaesthetic, interpersonal, intrapersonal, naturalistic
concepts.key_idea: Distinct intelligences work separately yet can cooperate on a real problem; each has a typical occupation profile.
concepts.textbook_ref: lepy101.txt, Theory of Multiple Intelligences (eight types from linguistic to naturalistic with example professions)
question_patterns: name the eight intelligences proposed by Gardner and one occupation suited to each
why does high musical intelligence fail to predict high logical-mathematical intelligence in Gardner's view?
which intelligence is shared by a surgeon and an athlete according to the theory of multiple intelligences?
how do the separate intelligences interact when a person solves an everyday problem?
identify the intelligence that poets and writers display most strongly in Gardner's framework
which intelligence involves awareness of our relationship with the natural world?

solution_steps.action: verify the independence claim
solution_steps.explain: excellence in one intelligence does not necessarily indicate a high or low level of the others

solution_steps.action: verify the cooperation claim
solution_steps.explain: the different intelligences interact and work together to find a solution to a single problem

worked_examples.q: How many relatively independent intelligences does Gardner's theory list?

concepts.title: Sternberg's Triarchic Theory of Intelligence
concepts.definition: Sternberg reads intelligent behaviour as adapting to, shaping and selecting environments, and splits it into three strands: componential analysis that serves school success, creative use of experience on fresh problems, and practical coping with daily demands.
concepts.key_idea: Analytical intelligence predicts school grades, creative intelligence handles novel problems, and practical intelligence is street-smart dealing with the environment.
concepts.textbook_ref: lepy101.txt, Triarchic Theory of Intelligence (three components, knowledge acquisition / meta / performance sub-components)
question_patterns: which component of the triarchic theory best explains success in school examinations?
match the three intelligences of Sternberg with the labels analytical, creative and practical
why is contextual intelligence described as street smartness or business sense?
name the three components that work inside componential intelligence
how does experiential intelligence reveal itself when a person meets a novel problem?
in what sense does Sternberg treat intelligent people as shapers of their environment?

solution_steps.action: verify the three-strand division
solution_steps.explain: componential, experiential and contextual are the basic types, each answering a different demand

solution_steps.action: verify the sub-components of componential intelligence
solution_steps.explain: knowledge acquisition, the higher-order meta component for planning, and the performance component that executes

worked_examples.q: Which Sternberg strand is street-smart coping with daily demands: componential, experiential or contextual?

concepts.title: PASS Model of Intelligence
concepts.definition: Das, Naglieri and Kirby picture intellect as three brain-based functional units - arousal with attention, coding done either simultaneously or successively, and planning - all operating over a knowledge base; their Cognitive Assessment System tests these processes in ages 5 to 18.
concepts.key_idea: Optimal arousal focuses attention, simultaneous processing integrates relations at once while successive processing stores information in sequence, and planning steers action to the goal.
concepts.textbook_ref: lepy101.txt, PASS model (functional units of brain, Raven's Progressive Matrices as simultaneous example, CAS battery)
question_patterns: explain the role of arousal and attention in the PASS model of intelligence
how does simultaneous processing differ from successive processing - give one test or task for each
why is planning treated as an essential feature of intelligence in the PASS model?
which test battery did Das and Naglieri develop to measure the PASS processes?
relate the three functional units of the brain to intellectual activity as the PASS model describes
give one example of school learning that demands successive processing of information

solution_steps.action: verify the processing contrast
solution_steps.explain: simultaneous processing perceives relations among concepts and merges them into one meaningful pattern, while successive processing recalls information serially so one item triggers the next

solution_steps.action: verify the planning loop
solution_steps.explain: plans are made, implemented against a target, evaluated, and modified when they fail to work

worked_examples.q: What does the P in the PASS model of intelligence stand for?

concepts.title: Twin-Study Correlations: Nature and Nurture in Intelligence
concepts.definition: Evidence on how intelligence develops comes from twin and adoption figures: the closer the genetic bond and the more similar the rearing setting, the higher the correlation between two people's intelligence scores, which supports a joint heredity-environment account.
concepts.key_idea: Identical twins reared together correlate near 0.90 while siblings reared apart correlate near 0.25, so genes set a range that environment fills in.
concepts.textbook_ref: lepy101.txt, Intelligence: Interplay of Nature and Nurture (0.90, 0.72, 0.60, 0.50, 0.25 correlation figures; adoption findings)
question_patterns: compare the intelligence correlation of identical twins reared together with that of siblings reared apart
using the twin study figures, find how much higher the identical-together correlation is than the fraternal-together one
what do adoption studies show about children's intelligence relative to biological and adoptive parents?
arrange the twin correlations reported for intelligence in decreasing order
why do psychologists conclude that intelligence arises from an interaction of heredity and environment?
compute the difference between the correlation for identical twins reared apart and fraternal twins reared together

solution_steps.action: subtract the fraternal-together correlation from the identical-together correlation
solution_steps.explain: both pairs share the rearing home, so the gap isolates the extra genetic overlap of identical twins

solution_steps.action: add the rearing effect to reach the siblings-apart comparison
solution_steps.explain: moving from siblings together (about 0.50) to siblings apart (about 0.25) adds the environmental separation effect onto the genetic gap

worked_examples.q: Identical twins reared together correlate near what value in intelligence studies? (Give one decimal.)

concepts.title: Aptitude: Nature and Measurement
concepts.definition: Aptitude is a person's specific capacity to acquire a particular skill after training; it differs from intelligence (general mental ability) and from interest (mere preference), and it is measured with independent tests or multi-area batteries such as the DAT and GATB.
concepts.key_idea: Aptitude predicts future performance; without both aptitude and interest in the same field, the outcome stays unsatisfactory.
concepts.textbook_ref: lepy101.txt, Aptitude: Nature and Measurement (independent vs multiple aptitude tests, DAT's 8 subtests, Ojha's Indian adaptation)
question_patterns: how is aptitude different from interest and from intelligence?
name the eight subtests of the Differential Aptitude Tests
why can a person who is keen on a job still fail for want of aptitude for it?
give two examples of independent aptitude tests used in vocational guidance
what does a high mechanical aptitude score predict about a student after training?
which well-known aptitude batteries exist in multiple or generalised form?

solution_steps.action: verify the prediction claim
solution_steps.explain: aptitude tests state what an individual will be able to do given proper training and a suitable environment

solution_steps.action: verify the two-part pairing condition
solution_steps.explain: success in a field needs aptitude and interest together - either one without the other yields an unsatisfactory outcome

worked_examples.q: What is a person's specific capacity to acquire a particular skill after training called?

concepts.title: Creativity and Its Relation to Intelligence
concepts.definition: Creativity is the power to bring forth something novel, appropriate and useful - a fresh solution, invention or composition; it rests on some minimum intellectual base, but past that base higher intelligence does not by itself ensure creative work.
concepts.formula: creative_output -> novelty plus usefulness ; requires minimum_intelligence, beyond_base no strict_correlation
concepts.key_idea: Intelligence tests reward convergent thinking with one right answer, while open-ended creativity tests reward divergent thinking that runs in many directions.
concepts.textbook_ref: lepy101.txt, Creativity and Intelligence (Terman 1920s findings, divergent vs convergent thinking, creativity testers Guilford and Torrance)
question_patterns: why is a high IQ no guarantee of creativity - answer with Terman's follow-up findings
contrast the convergent thinking of intelligence tests with the divergent thinking measured by creativity tests
how do heredity and environment jointly decide the level of creative potential a person reaches?
give one example each of creativity at the highest level and at the level of modifying what already exists
what abilities do open-ended creativity tests assess in a person?
explain, using a bright but reproductive student versus an average but improvising one, why intelligence alone misses creativity

solution_steps.action: verify the threshold claim
solution_steps.explain: a certain minimum level of intelligence is needed to acquire and organise knowledge, so the two are positively related up to that base

solution_steps.action: verify the independence beyond the base
solution_steps.explain: beyond the threshold, higher intelligence does not correlate well with creativity - highly intelligent children may show either high or low creativity

worked_examples.q: Which thinking does an intelligence test reward: convergent or divergent?

worked_examples.problem: A 10-year-old child attains a mental age of 12 on an intelligence scale. Work out the child's IQ.

steps.action: divide mental age by chronological age

worked_examples.answer: iq = 120, which places the child above the age norm since mental age exceeds chronological age

worked_examples.problem: A 12-year-old scores an IQ of 90. Recover the mental age behind the score.

steps.action: divide by 100 to land on the mental age

worked_examples.answer: mental_age_value = 10.8, i.e. the child performs like an average child of about 10 years 9-10 months, below the age norm

worked_examples.problem: A district has 50000 residents. Using the standard IQ classification, how many residents are expected to fall below IQ 70 (the intellectually disabled band, 2.2 percent)?

steps.action: multiply the population by the band percentage
convert percent into a head count

worked_examples.answer: band_count = 1100 residents in the intellectually disabled band
